story: Bulgaria is the poorest country in the EU, and between 2021 and 2026 it held eight parliamentary elections, none producing a government that lasted more than about a year. In December 2025, some 100,000 people, many of them young, filled the square outside parliament in Sofia to protest a budget and a political class they saw as captured by oligarchs. The government fell. On 1 January, Bulgaria adopted the euro anyway, becoming the eurozone's 21st member with no budget in place.

Into that vacuum stepped Rumen Radev, a former fighter pilot who had been the largely ceremonial president since 2017. He resigned the presidency in January, founded Progressive Bulgaria in March, and on 19 April won 44.7 percent and 131 of 240 seats, the first single-party majority since 1997 (Al Jazeera). Boyko Borissov's GERB, which had dominated Bulgarian politics for 15 years, fell to about 13 percent. Parliament approved Radev as prime minister on 8 May by 124 votes to 70 (AP via WTOP). He campaigned on dismantling the "mafia state" and lowering prices, criticised the euro switch and is seen as friendlier to Moscow than his predecessors, though analysts expect him to stay moderate because Bulgaria depends heavily on EU money. Critics noted his party later voted against measures targeting Delyan Peevski, the sanctioned oligarch he had campaigned against. A presidential election is due in November.
briefing.power: A parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the majority in the 240-seat National Assembly; the directly elected president is largely ceremonial but appoints caretaker governments when parliament deadlocks, which is why the office mattered so much in recent years.
briefing.holders: Prime Minister Rumen Radev (Progressive Bulgaria), in office since May 2026.
